sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the Church as a woman and a tower
sections.b: In the Visions of the Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, 100s) the Church appears to Hermas as a woman who changes with the believers' state: very old and seated, then younger, then young and joyful, then a young woman in white 'as if she were coming out of a bridal room' (Shepherd of Hermas 2:2; 18:3-5; 23:1). She is old 'because she was created first of all', and 'the world was put in order for her sake' (8:1), the same idea as 2 Clement's 'first church, the spiritual one, which was created before the sun and moon' (2 Clement 14:1). She also shows Hermas a tower being built on the water and says, 'The tower that you see being built is I myself, the Church' (11:3). Its stones are believers; those that fit perfectly are 'the apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons' (13:1); the tower stands on water 'because your life was saved through water' (11:5). The book tells the tower a second time in Similitude 9 (Shepherd of Hermas 78-110), there on a rock with a gate that is the Son of God.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 2:2; Shepherd of Hermas 8:1; 11:3; 11:5; 13:1; 18:3-5; 23:1; 2 Clement 14:1; Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Peter 2:5; Galatians 4:26

uncommon: The Shepherd of Hermas says the Church was created before the world, and the world was made for her (Shepherd of Hermas 8:1).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: one more chance, with a deadline
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas is built around repentance after baptism. In Vision 2 Hermas is given a message: all the sins of the saints 'up to this day' will be forgiven if they repent with all their heart; but God has sworn that 'if anyone sins any more now that this day has been set, he will not be saved', for 'the days of repentance are over for all the saints', while for the unbaptized nations 'there is repentance until the last day' (Shepherd of Hermas 6:4-5). Lake calls this 'the main point of the Shepherd' and reads it against Hebrews 6, where it is impossible to renew the fallen to repentance. In Vision 3 the deadline is the finishing of the tower: those who repent 'now, while the tower is being built' will be built in (13:5), and even the rejected stones 'have repentance', but only for 'a much lower' place after torment (15:5-6). Tertullian later scorned the book as 'the only one which favours adulterers' (On Modesty 10).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 6:4-5; 13:5; 15:5-6; Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; Hebrews 12:17

uncommon: The Shepherd of Hermas allows the baptized one repentance for sins committed up to the day of its revelation, and no more (Shepherd of Hermas 6:5).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: a Roman Christian's book
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas opens in Rome: Hermas, a former slave, is sold 'to a woman named Rhoda in Rome' and later sees her bathing in the Tiber (Shepherd of Hermas 1:1-2). His visions come on the road to Cumae (1:3; 5:1), in a field in the country (9:2), and on the Campanian Way (22:2). The old woman orders the book read 'in this city with the elders who lead the church', and sent by Clement 'to the cities abroad' (8:3). Lake dates it, with the Muratorian list, to the time Pius led the Roman church, about 148, and reports that 'many critics' think it was written over the twenty or thirty years before.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: a former slave writes
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas begins, 'The man who raised me sold me to a woman named Rhoda in Rome' (Shepherd of Hermas 1:1). Lake: 'presumably the meaning is that Hermas was born a slave, and that his owner sold him to Rhoda'. The author, once property, calls every believer 'a slave of God' (2:4; 22:3), and his Church tells those who serve the seven virtues that they serve them 'like a slave' (16:8).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: an apocalypse about repentance
sections.b: Lake: the Shepherd 'is in form an apocalypse', revelations made 'by the Church, who appears in the form of a woman', by the Shepherd and by a great angel, but 'its object is practical and ethical'. Its Visions use the forms of Jewish and Christian apocalypse: a spirit that carries the seer off, the sky opened, a heavenly book, fasting before revelation, angels who explain, and a beast with fiery locusts whose four colors map the end of the world (Shepherd of Hermas 1:3-4; 5:3-4; 6:1; 22:6; 24:2-5). Hermas first takes the woman for the Sibyl (8:1).

sections.h: Clement in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: In the Shepherd of Hermas the Church tells Hermas to make two copies of his little book and send one 'to Clement', who 'will send it to the cities abroad, for that is the task given to him' (Shepherd of Hermas 8:3). Lake (introduction to 1 Clement): this 'certainly points to a Clement in Rome exercising the same functions as the writer of I. Clement; but Hermas is probably somewhat later than I. Clement, and the reference may be merely a literary device based on knowledge of the earlier book.'

sections.h: Grapte and the widows in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: In Rome the Shepherd of Hermas is to be sent to a woman named Grapte, who 'will instruct the widows and the orphans' (Shepherd of Hermas 8:3). The church's care for widows and orphans is James's 'clean and unspoiled religion' (James 1:27); whether Grapte held an office like the enrolled widows of 1 Timothy 5:9-10, the text does not say.

sections.h: The round stones in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: In Vision 3 of the Shepherd of Hermas white round stones lie beside the tower, unfit for building: believers who 'have faith, but who also have the wealth of this world', and in persecution 'deny their Lord because of their wealth and their business dealings'. They will be useful only 'when the wealth that leads them astray is cut away from them', as a round stone must be trimmed to be square (Shepherd of Hermas 14:5-6). Hermas himself is the example: 'When you were rich, you were no use, but now you are useful' (14:7). The Church warns the rich to seek out the hungry before the tower is finished (17:5-6).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 14:5-7; 17:2-6; Matthew 13:22; Mark 10:23-25; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; James 5:1-4

sections.h: The beast of the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: In Vision 4 of the Shepherd of Hermas a beast 'like some sea monster', a hundred feet long, with fiery locusts coming from its mouth, rushes at Hermas on a country road; he puts on faith, walks toward it, and it lies down and lets him pass (Shepherd of Hermas 22:6-9). The angel Thegri 'who is over the beasts' shut its mouth (23:4), and its four colors (black, fire and blood, gold, white) stand for this world, its destruction, the faithful tested, and the age to come (24:2-5). The Church says it is 'a figure of the great suffering that is coming' (23:5).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 22:6-10; 23:4-5; 24:2-5; Revelation 13:1; Daniel 7:3; Daniel 6:22

sections.h: Angels in the Visions of Hermas
sections.b: In the Shepherd of Hermas young men are angels. Six 'holy angels of God who were created first' build the tower, with countless angels under them, and the Lord 'handed over his whole creation to them' (Shepherd of Hermas 12:1-2). A handsome young man reveals that the old woman is the Church (8:1); another explains her three forms (18:7-21:4). An angel named Thegri, 'who is over the beasts', shuts the beast's mouth, as in Daniel 6:22 (23:4). Lake notes that no other mention of Thegri is found in Jewish or Christian literature. Those who stand firm will 'pass in with the holy angels' (6:7).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 6:7; 8:1; 12:1-2; 18:7; 23:4; Tobit 12:15; 1 Enoch 20:1-8; Daniel 6:22

sections.h: The right side of the couch: martyrs in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: When Hermas tries to sit on the right, the Church stops him: the place on the right belongs to 'those who have already pleased God and have suffered for the sake of the Name', who bore 'whips, prisons, great sufferings, crosses, and wild beasts'. Yet both sides have 'the same gifts and the same promises'; those on the right 'have a certain glory' (Shepherd of Hermas 9:9-10:1). In the tower the stones dragged from the deep are 'the ones who have suffered for the name of the Lord' (13:2).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 9:9; 10:1; 13:2; Matthew 20:21-23; Acts 5:41; Hebrews 11:36-37

sections.h: The great suffering in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas expects a persecution soon. 'Blessed are you, all who endure the great suffering that is coming, and all who will not deny their life' (Shepherd of Hermas 6:7); Maximus, whose 'deny again' implies that he had denied once, is told, 'Look, suffering is coming. If you think it best, deny again' (7:4). The beast of Vision 4 is 'a figure of the great suffering that is coming', and the faithful can escape it by repenting with all their heart (23:5); 'if you are willing, it will be nothing' (24:6). The Greek thlipsis is the word of Revelation 7:14.

sections.h: Elders and leaders in the Visions of Hermas
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas shows the church in Rome led by a group. Hermas is to read his book 'with the elders who lead the church' (Shepherd of Hermas 8:3), using the verb of 1 Timothy 5:17; the Church speaks to 'the leaders of the church' (6:6) and to 'you who lead the church and to you who take the front seats', warning them against quarrels (17:7-10). The best stones in the tower are 'the apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons' (13:1). The Church herself is 'the old woman', presbytera, the feminine of the word for elder (8:1).

sections.h: The Book of Eldad and Modad in the Shepherd of Hermas
sections.b: The only written source the Shepherd of Hermas names is a lost book: 'The Lord is near to those who turn back', 'as it is written in Eldad and Modat, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness' (Shepherd of Hermas 7:4). The two are the Eldad and Medad of Numbers 11:26. Lake: the book 'is mentioned among the Apocrypha of the N.T. in the Athanasian Synopsis and in the Stichometry of Nicephorus, but is not extant. It is thought to be quoted in II Clem. xi. 2.'
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 7:4; Numbers 11:26-29; 2 Clement 11:2; 1 Clement 23:3
